identity.title: Right lower quadrant pain with periumbilical-to-RLQ migration

technique.how: Ask where the pain started and where it is now, and whether it moved: classic migration is vague periumbilical or epigastric visceral pain that, over hours, localizes to the right lower quadrant as the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed. Establish timing relative to anorexia, nausea and vomiting (vomiting before pain argues against appendicitis).
technique.prerequisites: Patient able to give a history; ask open questions before leading ones.

interpretation.positive_finding: Migration of pain to the RLQ increases the likelihood of appendicitis (pediatric pooled LR+ 4.8 in undifferentiated abdominal pain); it is one of the three strongest history items in adult meta-analysis.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of migration lowers probability but is common in proven appendicitis (about half of children lack it), so it cannot exclude the diagnosis.
interpretation.pitfalls: Children and elderly patients localize poorly; retrocaecal or pelvic appendicitis may never migrate to McBurney point. Migration is not specific to appendicitis (e.g. cecal diverticulitis, perforated ulcer tracking down the right gutter).
interpretation.changes_what: Present: move toward appendicitis, obtain imaging or surgical review even if exam is mild. Absent: reduces but does not remove suspicion; rely on exam and inflammatory markers.

estimates.population: Children with undifferentiated abdominal pain in ED-based studies (subset of 21 studies, 8,605 patients, weighted prevalence 39.2% overall)
estimates.reference_standard: Surgical pathology, imaging or clinical follow-up as defined in included studies
estimates.quote: history of "pain migration to right lower quadrant (RLQ)" (LR+ = 4.81, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 3.59-6.44)

estimates.population: 755 children and adolescents with suspected appendicitis, 36% with appendicitis
estimates.computed_from: sensitivity = 1 - 0.50 (proportion of proven appendicitis cases with lack of migration of pain)

sources.citation: Benabbas R, Hanna M, Shah J, Sinert R. Diagnostic Accuracy of History, Physical Examination, Laboratory Tests, and Point-of-care Ultrasound for Pediatric Acute Appendicitis in the Emergency Department: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2017;24(5):523-551.
Kharbanda AB, Taylor GA, Fishman SJ, Bachur RG. Atypical clinical features of pediatric appendicitis. Acad Emerg Med. 2007;14(2):124-129.
Andersson RE. Meta-analysis of the clinical and laboratory diagnosis of appendicitis. Br J Surg. 2004;91(1):28-37.
Wagner JM, McKinney WP, Carpenter JL. Does this patient have appendicitis? JAMA. 1996;276(19):1589-1594.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of migration to exclude appendicitis in young children, the elderly, pregnant women, or patients with cognitive impairment or poor historians.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Migrating pain that becomes diffuse with fever, rigidity or hypotension suggests perforation: antibiotics, imaging and urgent surgical review.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Depends on recall and questioning style; Benabbas 2017 found the LR+ strong only in undifferentiated pain, not once appendicitis was already suspected (spectrum effect).

extraction_notes: Adult pooled LR for migration (Wagner 1996 RCE; Andersson 2004) sits in tables not visible via PubMed/PMC; both are cited qualitatively (Andersson abstract: migration among strongest discriminators). Numeric estimates come from pediatric ED evidence: Benabbas 2017 pooled LR+ 4.81 (3.59-6.44) in undifferentiated abdominal pain, and Kharbanda 2007 sensitivity 0.50 computed from the reported 50% of proven cases lacking migration. Laurell 2013 (PMID 23838773) reports OR 2.18 for migration (not entered).
